words.meaning: keen insight and the ability to understand things quickly and judge accurately
words.example: The reporter's perspicacity helped her spot the flaw in the official story.

words.meaning: the ability to notice subtle differences and make good, careful judgments
words.example: Good leadership requires the discernment to separate facts from noise.

words.meaning: a person who loves learning and studying
words.example: As a true philomath, she reads three books a week on subjects she knows nothing about.
His assiduity in the laboratory eventually produced a breakthrough the whole team celebrated.

words.meaning: a long, formal discussion or examination of one topic
words.example: Her new book is a brilliant disquisition on how memory shapes identity.
words.persian: بحث مفصل و رسمی دربارهٔ یک موضوع

words.meaning: close, critical interpretation of a written text
words.example: The professor's exegesis of the poem revealed meanings we had all missed.

words.meaning: obscure and difficult for most people to understand
words.example: His lecture was fascinating but so recondite that only specialists followed it.
words.persian: کمتر شناخته‌شده و دشوار برای فهم

words.meaning: a broad, comprehensive overview of a whole subject
words.example: The opening chapter offers a concise conspectus of two hundred years of scientific progress.
words.persian: بررسی جامع و خلاصهٔ یک موضوع

words.meaning: a structured series of questions and answers used for teaching
words.example: The new recruits memorized the company's safety catechism before entering the factory.

words.meaning: deep wisdom and good judgment that grows out of experience
words.example: Her sagacity as a negotiator saved the company from a disastrous merger.

grammar.title: 6A: Passive (all tenses)
grammar.explanation:
Use the **passive voice** when the action matters more than the doer. A true philomath reads a disquisition for its ideas, not for the hand that wrote it.

Build it with **be** plus the **past participle**. *Is decoded*, *was published*, *has been revised* — the old object becomes the new subject.

Name the agent with **by** only when it adds real information. *The recondite manuscript was cracked by a philomath* keeps the hero; otherwise drop it, as in *Mistakes were made*.

The passive works in every tense: **is being analyzed**, **had been hidden**, **will be taught**. Formal and academic writing favors it because it sounds objective and precise.

Common mistake: never use **by** when the agent is obvious or unknown. A conspectus *is written*, not *is written by someone*.
examples: *The recondite text was decoded* after months of assiduity. (focus on the result, not the reader)
*Her exegesis has been published* in three journals. (the agent is obvious from context)
*A conspectus of the whole field is being prepared* by the research team. (by names the agent on purpose)
*The questions in the catechism must be answered* with discernment. (modal + passive)
*If the code had not been broken*, the sealed room would have stayed hidden. (past perfect passive in conditionals)

practice.q: Turn into the passive: The librarian admired her perspicacity.
practice.a: Her perspicacity was admired by the librarian.

practice.q: Which is more formal: 'We translated the text' or 'The text was translated'?
practice.a: 'The text was translated' — the passive sounds more objective and formal.

practice.q: Fix the mistake: 'The conspectus has been wrote with great care.'
practice.a: 'The conspectus has been written with great care.'
